title: Financial Fraud and Scams
summary: Spot the costume → Run the scan → Act in the first hour → Lock the doors
subtitle: Slow the scam down before it speeds your money away

blocks.text: A scammer’s favourite financial product is urgency. It has no prospectus, no cooling-off period and comes with unlimited exclamation marks.

Canadians reported more than $704 million in fraud losses in 2025, a record. Police think only 5% to 10% of frauds are ever reported, so the real number is far higher. Fraud can arrive as a bank alert, a call from the government, a new romance, an investment tip, a job offer or a family emergency. The costume changes. The pressure pattern repeats.

This lesson gives you four tools: a field guide to today’s most common scams, a five-question scan, a first-hour plan if money or a code has already left, and a short setup that makes your household a harder target. None of it relies on blaming the person who was targeted.
A caller ID, email logo or familiar-looking website is not proof of identity. End the contact and verify through a phone number or website you locate independently.

items.title: “Only careless people fall for scams.”
items.text: Fraud is built to exploit trust, fear, hope, authority and time pressure. Anyone can be targeted. A rehearsed pause and check routine is more useful than shame.

blocks.text: Learn the costumes once, and you’ll spot them in every disguise.
blocks.detail: Most scams are a handful of old scripts in new clothes. Knowing the script lets you hang up early, before the pressure builds.
blocks.extra: Section 02 is a field guide to six scams Canadians meet most.

blocks.text: Each scam below has one tell, a request a real organization won’t make. Learn the tell, and you don’t need to win the argument on the phone.

items.title: THE BANK “INVESTIGATOR”
items.text: A caller from “fraud services” says your account is under attack and asks you to move money to a “safe account”, read out a code or hand your card to a courier. The tell: your bank won’t ask you to move money to protect it, and it won’t send anyone to pick up your card.

items.title: THE GOVERNMENT THREAT
items.text: A caller or text says you owe tax, your SIN is suspended or police are on the way. The tell: the Canada Revenue Agency won’t demand payment in gift cards, prepaid cards or crypto, and it won’t threaten you with arrest.

items.title: THE FAMILY EMERGENCY
items.text: A grandchild, child or friend is “in jail” or “in hospital” and needs cash now, and asks you to tell no one. Voices can now be cloned from short online clips. The tell: secrecy plus a courier or a cash pickup. Hang up and call the person on a number you already have.

items.title: THE ROMANCE
items.text: Someone you met online is warm, attentive and always just unable to meet or video chat. Then comes a crisis, a plane ticket or a can’t-miss investment. The tell: anyone you haven’t met in person who asks for money.

items.title: THE INVESTMENT
items.text: A celebrity ad, a group chat or a new friend shows huge returns on crypto or a trading app. Early “profits” look real, but withdrawing needs a fee or tax first. The tell: guaranteed high returns and a platform that isn’t registered. Check registration at aretheyregistered.ca.

items.title: THE JOB
items.text: An easy remote job pays for “rating products” or “processing payments”, but first you must top up an account, buy equipment or move money for the employer. The tell: a job that asks you to pay or to pass money through your account.

blocks.text: Money moved through your account for a stranger can make you a “money mule”. Even if you were fooled, your bank may close your account and you may have to repay the funds. Never let anyone use your account to receive or forward money.

Run five checks on any request for money, a code or a password. Source: did you start the contact? Time: are you being rushed? Offer: does the claim hold up to an independent check? Payment: does the method remove your usual protections? Credentials: are you being asked for a password, code or remote access? One red flag doesn’t prove fraud, but it earns a pause.

blocks.text: Read the pressure pattern

items.title: SOURCE
items.text: Did you start the contact through a channel you trust?

items.title: TIME
items.text: Are you being rushed, threatened or told to keep the request secret?

items.title: OFFER
items.text: Does the claim survive an independent check?

items.title: PAYMENT
items.text: Does the requested method remove your usual protections?

items.title: CREDENTIALS
items.text: Are you being asked for a password, PIN, one-time code, remote access or card pickup?

blocks.text: One-time passcodes are keys, not customer-service trivia. A legitimate code arriving on your device can still be part of a fraudster’s login attempt. Never read it to an unsolicited caller.

Scammers prefer payment methods you can’t reverse: gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, cash handed to a courier and, more and more, e-Transfers and instant payments. A credit card purchase can sometimes be disputed. Most of the others can’t.

items.title: “If the caller knows my name, bank and recent details, the call is genuine.”
items.text: Personal details can come from data breaches, social media, stolen mail or an earlier contact. Check independently, and never trust a caller just because they know things about you.

sections.title: Colin, the Bank Investigator and the Very Helpful Courier

blocks.text: Meet Colin
paragraphs: Colin Fraser is making supper in Winnipeg when his phone shows the name of his bank. The caller knows his full name. He says the fraud department has spotted a transfer. To protect Colin’s savings, he must move the money into a ‘secure account’ before the branch closes. The caller sounds calm and kind.

Then a real one-time code arrives by text. The caller asks Colin to read it aloud. Next he says a courier will collect Colin’s bank card as evidence. The potatoes are boiling over, the caller is counting down and the whole evening has become a low-budget thriller with excellent caller ID.

Colin remembers a family rule: no money, code or card leaves during a call we didn’t start. He hangs up, even though the caller warns that the transfer will be final. He calls the number on the back of his card. The bank says it never called, and it locks the attempted login. Colin changes his password on a safe device and turns on a stronger login check.

He saves the number, text, time and his notes without clicking anything. He follows the bank’s instructions, reports the call to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and tells local police as needed. He also tells his sister, who got a similar call that week.

Two days later, someone offers to recover money for an upfront fee. Colin has lost no money, but this second caller has plenty of optimism and an invoice ready. Colin refuses and adds the contact to his report. He did not outsmart every scam. He used a routine that works under stress: pause, leave the channel, verify, protect and report.

blocks.text: Recovery scams often target people who were already contacted or harmed. A caller who knows details from the first incident does not prove they are a real recovery service. Check independently, and never send an upfront payment under pressure.
What resolved the conflict?
Colin used a family rule he had decided in advance, a trusted way to reach the bank and fast account protection. The routine broke the pressure cycle. Perfect confidence did not.
Colin’s rule cost him nothing and saved his account, because he had decided it before he ever needed it.
blocks.detail: The first hour after a scam decides what can still be stopped. A plan made now keeps that hour calm.
blocks.extra: Section 05 walks through the first hour, minute by minute.

sections.title: The First Hour, Minute by Minute

blocks.text: If money, a code, a card or remote access has already left your hands, speed matters more than embarrassment. Payments can sometimes be stopped or recalled in the first minutes or hours. Work down this list in order.
Your first-hour file

items.title: Minute 0: Stop
items.text: End the call or chat. If anyone is in danger, call 911. Don’t meet a courier or keep talking to gather evidence.

items.title: Minute 5: Call the bank
items.text: Use the number on your card or the bank’s website. Ask them to freeze, recall or dispute the payment, and to lock your card and online banking.

items.title: Minute 15: Lock access
items.text: From a clean device, change your email password first, then banking. Sign out of all sessions and turn on MFA. If you gave remote access, disconnect that device from the internet.

items.title: Minute 30: Save evidence
items.text: Write a short timeline. Keep numbers, texts, emails, receipts, transaction IDs and screenshots. Don’t reply to the scammer.

items.title: Minute 45: Report
items.text: Call local police and get a file number. Report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre online or at 1-888-495-8501, even if you lost nothing.

items.title: Minute 60: Protect your ID
items.text: If you shared your SIN, ID or card details, ask Equifax and TransUnion for a fraud alert on your credit file. Each bureau must be asked separately.

blocks.text: Who to call, and why
Your recovery contacts
blocks.detail: Write these down before you need them

items.title: Your bank or card issuer
items.text: First — only they can freeze an account, recall a payment or start a dispute.

items.title: Local police
items.text: Second — a police file number helps with banks, credit bureaus and insurers.

items.title: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre
items.text: 1-888-495-8501 — or report online. Reports link cases and warn others.

items.title: Equifax and TransUnion
items.text: Fraud alert — asks lenders to check it’s you before opening new credit.

blocks.text: Got a scam text? Don’t tap the link or reply STOP. Forward it to 7726 (SPAM) so your carrier can block the sender, then delete it.
Reporting an attempted scam still matters. It can connect patterns, warn others and support investigations even when no money left your account.

items.title: “Once money is sent, reporting is pointless.”
items.text: Recovery is not guaranteed, but acting fast may improve the chance of stopping or tracing a payment. Reporting also creates records that help investigators. Act quickly, and beware anyone promising recovery for an upfront fee.

sections.title: Lock the Doors Before Anyone Knocks

blocks.text: The best time to beat a scam is a calm Sunday afternoon, long before the phone rings. These five steps take about an hour and make your household a much harder target.

items.title: Set a family code word
items.text: Pick a word that isn’t online anywhere. Anyone asking for emergency money must say it. No word, no money.

items.title: Save the real numbers
items.text: Store your bank’s fraud line, your card issuer and two trusted people in your phone, labelled clearly, so you never have to search for a number under pressure.

items.title: Harden your email
items.text: Your email resets every other password. Give it a long, unique password and turn on MFA, preferably an authenticator app instead of text codes.

items.title: Turn on alerts and limits
items.text: Set your bank to text you for every e-Transfer and large purchase. Lower your daily transfer limit if you rarely move big amounts.

items.title: Name a trusted contact
items.text: Your investment firm must ask you for a trusted contact person it can call if it sees signs of fraud or confusion. Fill that in, and check whether your bank offers something similar.

blocks.text: Talk about scams with older relatives the way you’d talk about the weather: often and without judgement. People who feel ashamed hide losses, and hidden losses keep growing.

items.title: “I’m too smart to get scammed.”
items.text: Scams are built to work on tired, busy, worried and hopeful people, which is all of us on some days. A routine you’ve practised beats confidence every time.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why is a separate channel essential for verification?
items.detail: You leave the suspicious contact and reach the real organization through contact details you found yourself.

items.title: Name three pressure signals that justify a pause.
items.detail: Rushing, secrecy, threats, someone pretending to be someone else, odd payment methods or requests for codes and passwords.

items.title: What should you do with an unexpected one-time passcode request?
items.detail: Do not share it. End the contact and verify independently.

items.title: What are the first two organizations to contact after money is transferred fraudulently?
items.detail: The bank or payment provider right away, then local police or the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre as needed.

items.title: Why report attempted fraud and recovery scams?
items.detail: Reports connect patterns, warn others, support investigations and document follow-up activity.

items.title: A caller from your bank says to move your savings to a “safe account” to protect it. What do you do?
items.detail: Hang up and call the number on your card. Banks don’t ask you to move money to protect it.

items.title: A job offer asks you to receive money and send it on. What is the risk?
items.detail: You could be used as a money mule. Your account could be closed, and you may have to repay the money.

blocks.text: Preserve facts, not shame: what contact arrived, what was shared, what moved, when it happened and what protection followed.

sections.title: Your Action: Household Scam Response Card

blocks.text: Write down who to contact, not passwords, PINs, one-time codes, full card numbers or security answers.
A household code word can confirm a real family emergency. Confirm it through another known contact too, and don’t let an urgent voice message appoint itself chief financial officer.
Urgency is the signal to slow down, not speed up.
blocks.detail: Pause on incoming requests, check through a separate trusted channel, protect accounts quickly and report the facts without shame. A rehearsed routine works better than perfect confidence.

items.title: Phishing
items.text: A fake message or site meant to trick you into giving up information, money or access.

items.title: Spoofing
items.text: Faking the caller, sender or website details you see, to look trustworthy.

items.title: Social engineering
items.text: Tricking people through emotion, trust or pressure, not just through technical attacks.

items.title: One-time passcode
items.text: A temporary code used to confirm access or a payment. Do not share it with anyone who contacts you out of the blue.

items.title: Recovery scam
items.text: A follow-up fraud that promises to get your money back, often for an upfront fee.

items.title: MFA
items.text: Multi-factor authentication: more than one type of proof is needed to open an account.

items.title: Money mule
items.text: A person whose account is used to receive and pass on stolen money, often without knowing it is a crime.

items.title: Fraud alert
items.text: A note on your credit file that asks lenders to confirm your identity before opening new credit in your name.

questions: What is your household’s rule for any request for money, codes or passwords that comes in by call, text or email?

Where will you keep your bank’s real phone number, and which two people will you call for a quick pause-and-check?
Which accounts need a unique password and stronger MFA? Start with email and banking.
Which bank alerts or limits will you turn on this week?
What would you save as evidence if you were scammed, and when will you hold a 10-minute scam drill?
